title: Pareto front: what are the trade-offs?
summary: When there are two goals that conflict, there is usually no single best design: there is a front of designs where improving one goal costs the other. The Pareto plot shows all candidates, marks the non-dominated ones, and points out the knee.

media.alt: Scatter plot of objective 1 against objective 2, both to be minimised: many grey crosses (dominated) above and to the right, twelve teal dots joined by a dashed staircase (non-dominated) running from upper left to lower right, and an amber circle marking the knee near (0.22, 0.78).
media.caption: Reference render of class F7.4 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: What are the trade-offs?
read_the_figure.axes: x: objective 1 (minimise). y: objective 2 (minimise). Both linear, scaled to about 0 to 1. The lower left is better.
look_at: Which points have no other point below and to the left of them? Those are the front.
How steep is the front in different places: where is a small loss of one goal buying a large gain in the other?
Where is the knee, and why is it there?
How many points are dominated and how many are not (are the counts shown)?
as_drawn: Ninety candidates: 78 dominated (grey crosses) and 12 non-dominated (teal dots), counts shown in the legend.
The dashed teal staircase joins the 12 front points and marks the boundary of the region that the candidates dominate.
The amber circle marks the knee at about (0.22, 0.78): the front point farthest from the straight line joining the two extreme points, at a distance of about 0.07.
Both axes say minimise, and the lower left corner is best; there is no point in the lower left corner, which is the trade-off.
read_the_figure.proves: The non-dominated set is exactly the set of candidates for which no other candidate is at least as good in both goals and strictly better in one. Choosing among them needs a value judgement the plot cannot supply.
if_wrong: A dominated point drawn as part of the front: check the dominance test and ties.
Objectives with different units or scales on the axes: the knee and the visual trade-off change with scaling.
A maximise goal plotted as if minimise: the front is then mirrored.
must_check: dominated vs non-dominated: the distinction is the content of the figure; without it the plot is just a scatter.
knee marked: the knee is the usual candidate when no preference is given, and the reader should see which point it is and how it was chosen.

terms.meaning: A quantity to be minimised (or maximised) by the design.
Design a dominates design b if it is no worse in every objective and strictly better in at least one.
The set of non-dominated designs: the best available trade-offs.
A point on the front where a small improvement in one objective costs a large loss in the other; commonly the point farthest from the line joining the extremes.
The rate at which one objective must be given up to improve the other.

remember: a dominates b if f_i(a) <= f_i(b) for all i and f_j(a) < f_j(b) for some j.
The front is the set of points that nothing dominates.
Knee: maximise the distance d = |cross(b - a, p - a)| / |b - a| from the line through the extremes a and b.
Rescale objectives before judging the knee by eye.
Weighted sums find only the convex part of a front.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Each point is one candidate design placed by its two objective values. Grey crosses are dominated; teal dots are non-dominated; a dashed staircase joins the dots; an amber ring marks the knee. Shape and colour both carry the dominated or non-dominated distinction, so it survives greyscale. Counts of each group appear in the legend.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: if two things matter and they pull in opposite directions there is no best design, only a set of sensible compromises. Plotting each design as a point shows every compromise and lets you see which designs are simply bad (anything with another point to its lower left). What is left, the front, is the honest menu of trade-offs. The knee marks a natural default.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: The picture depends on the scaling of the axes: rescale one objective and the knee moves. The staircase suggests that points between the dots are attainable, which is not necessarily true. The front found is only the front of the candidates sampled, not of the problem. A knee is a geometric convenience, not a statement about what you value. With three or more objectives the picture does not extend.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: For three or more objectives use a parallel-coordinates plot or a scatter-plot matrix with the front highlighted. A table of the front sorted by one objective with the trade-off rate between neighbours is more precise. A weighted-sum or a constraint form (minimise one subject to a bound on the other) may be what a decision needs.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Normalise both objectives to 0 to 1, shade the dominated region, annotate the slope between neighbouring front points, and let a slider for the weight on objective 1 move a marker along the front.

steps.title: Dominance
steps.tex: a\prec b\iff f_i(a)\le f_i(b)\ \forall i\ \text{and}\ f_j(a)<f_j(b)\ \text{for some }j
steps.note: The front is {a : no b dominates a}. In the render this leaves 12 of 90 candidates.

steps.title: Knee by distance to the extreme line
steps.note: With a the leftmost and b the rightmost front point; for the render's data the maximum is d = 0.068 at (0.222, 0.784).

steps.title: Trade-off rate between neighbours
steps.note: Between (0.22, 0.785) and (0.295, 0.745) the rate is 0.5; between (0.775, 0.39) and (0.825, 0.27) it is 2.4: the last stretch is expensive.

worked.title: Reading the Pareto front in the reference render
worked.problem: (1) How many points are on the front and what is the test? (2) Is a design at (0.5, 0.8) dominated? (3) What are the trade-off rates just left and just right of the knee?

solution.text: (1) The legend gives 12 non-dominated and 78 dominated. A point is on the front if no other point is below and to the left of it (or equal in one coordinate and better in the other).
(2) Yes. The front point at (0.295, 0.745) has both objectives smaller, so it dominates (0.5, 0.8).
(3) From (0.115, 0.915) to the knee (0.22, 0.785) the rate is 1.2. From the knee to (0.295, 0.745) it is 0.53.
Left of the knee, a unit of objective 1 buys more than a unit of objective 2; right of it, less: the knee is where the exchange rate changes from favourable to unfavourable for the first goal.

worked.answer: 12 front points; yes, (0.5, 0.8) is dominated by (0.295, 0.745); the trade-off rate changes from about 1.2 to 0.5 across the knee.

analyze.q: How would the knee change if objective 2 were measured in different units (multiplied by 10)?
analyze.hint: The distance to the line depends on scaling.

analyze.q: Why is the dashed staircase not a promise that designs exist on it?
analyze.hint: Only the plotted points are known designs.

analyze.q: What does the empty lower left corner tell you?

evaluate.q: You must hand a single design to a client. Is the knee the right one?

create: Redraw with both objectives normalised and the dominated region shaded.
Add a third objective as colour and check which front points stay non-dominated.

checks.q: What does it mean that a point is dominated?
checks.hint: Compare with another point in both objectives.
checks.answer: Another design is at least as good in both objectives and strictly better in one, so there is no reason to prefer the dominated one.

checks.q: Points (0.2, 0.6), (0.3, 0.5), (0.4, 0.7) with both objectives minimised. Which are on the front?
checks.answer: (0.2, 0.6) and (0.3, 0.5) are on the front; (0.4, 0.7) is dominated by both.

checks.q: Two analysts pick different knees from the same data. What could explain it?
checks.answer: They scaled the objectives differently or used a different definition of the knee; the knee depends on the units of the axes, so normalise and state the definition.
